definition.text: The branch of economics that studies how a whole economy, regional, national or global, performs and behaves.

facts.text: Macroeconomists study economy-wide totals such as GDP, national income, unemployment, inflation, consumption, saving, investment and trade.
Its three central variables are output, unemployment and inflation.
It differs from microeconomics, which studies smaller units such as single firms, consumers and markets.
Its topics split by time frame: short-term swings of the business cycle, medium-term levels of variables such as unemployment, and long-term growth.
It also analyses monetary and fiscal policy, especially where they aim to stabilize the economy or its growth rate.
As a separate field it is usually dated to 1936, when Keynes published The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money.
Everything produced and sold generates an equal amount of income, and total net output is usually measured as GDP.
Since World War II, Keynesians, monetarists, new classical and new Keynesian economists have shaped mainstream research.

definition.text: Inflation is a general rise in prices across a whole economy; deflation is a general fall in prices.

facts.text: Economists measure these price changes with price indexes.
Inflation rises when an economy overheats and grows too fast, and a shrinking economy can push inflation down or into deflation.
Supply shocks also move inflation, for example the oil crises of the 1970s and the 2021–2023 global energy crisis.
High inflation and deflation both raise uncertainty, especially when unexpected, so most central banks aim for low, stable, positive inflation.
The quantity theory of money says price changes are caused by changes in the money supply, but it has proved unreliable over short and medium horizons.

definition.text: The state of people in the labour force who have no job but are actively looking for one, measured as a percentage called the unemployment rate.

facts.text: Retired people, students and discouraged job-seekers are outside the labour force and are not counted as unemployed.
Unemployment has a cyclical part that follows the business cycle and a lasting structural, or natural, part.
Okun's law links unemployment to short-run GDP growth; its original version says a 3% rise in output cuts unemployment by 1%.
Search, or frictional, unemployment arises because matching workers to vacancies takes time when information is imperfect.
Minimum wages, trade unions and efficiency wages can keep wages above the level where supply equals demand, causing some unemployment.

definition.text: The total amount of money in an economy, commonly measured as M1 and M2.

facts.text: M1 is liquid money such as cash, coins and checking deposits; M2 adds less liquid items such as time deposits, savings accounts and money market funds.
A liquid asset can be turned into cash quickly without much loss of value.
The money supply affects interest rates and is central to monetary policy.

definition.text: The school of thought begun by Keynes's General Theory, which explains why markets might not clear and stresses total demand as the driver of output.

facts.text: During the Great Depression, economists of the time struggled to explain how goods could go unsold and workers stay unemployed.
The older neoclassical view held that prices and wages would fall until all goods and labour were sold.
Keynes argued that a return to normal output would be slow at best, and he recommended active fiscal policy to stabilize demand and employment.
Keynes's followers merged his ideas with neoclassical microeconomics into the neoclassical synthesis, accepted by most economists by the 1950s.

definition.text: The way a change in spending is magnified as it passes through the economy, raising or lowering total output by more than the original change.

facts.text: Keynes explained how a small fall in consumption or investment could be magnified into declines across the economy.
A government-paid bridge adds its own value to output and also lets the workers spend and invest more, helping close an output gap.

definition.text: Milton Friedman's school of macroeconomics, which updated the quantity theory of money and stressed money's role in the economy.

facts.text: Friedman argued monetary policy was more effective than fiscal policy, but favoured steady money-supply growth over frequent intervention.
Friedman and Edmund Phelps denied a stable long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment, a view supported by the 1970s oil shocks.
It was influential in the early 1980s but faded when central banks found money growth, inflation and real GDP growth too unstably linked to target money.

definition.text: The assumption, brought into macroeconomics by Robert Lucas, that people form forecasts using all current information about policy and conditions rather than just recent past trends.

facts.text: Before Lucas, economists used adaptive expectations, where people look only at the recent past.
In new classical models with rational expectations, monetary policy had only a limited effect.
The Lucas critique argued that models built on past statistical relationships fail when the underlying economy changes, and called for models with microeconomic foundations.

definition.text: A macroeconomic school that accepts rational expectations but shows how sticky prices and wages let monetary and fiscal policy affect real output.

facts.text: It traces sticky prices and wages to imperfect competition, so monetary policy changes quantities rather than only prices.
Stanley Fischer and John B. Taylor showed monetary policy could work even under rational expectations when contracts fix wages.

definition.text: A model of long-run economic growth, worked out by Robert Solow and Trevor Swan in the 1950s, in which output is produced from capital and labour.

facts.text: It remains a common textbook model of long-run growth.
Output grows only through more capital, a larger population, or technology that raises total factor productivity.
Saving more raises output only temporarily, because depreciation eventually uses up savings in replacing worn-out capital.
In the model, growth in output per person depends only on technological progress.
It followed the 1940s Harrod–Domar model and is a special case of the Ramsey model, in which saving is chosen by households.

definition.text: Growth models from the 1980s and 1990s that explain growth from inside the economy, through increasing returns, learning-by-doing or firms' research, instead of outside technological change.

facts.text: Some versions model profit-seeking firms' research and development to explain technological progress.

title: Environment in macroeconomic models

definition.text: The inclusion of natural resource scarcity and climate change in macroeconomic models, especially growth models, to study their effects on the whole economy.

facts.text: Jevons's 1865 book The Coal Question argued that productivity gains could speed up resource scarcity in a growing economy.
During the 1970s oil crises, Stiglitz and Solow added non-renewable resources to growth models to ask whether living standards could keep rising.
The 2006 Stern Review gave the first comprehensive analysis of global economic damage from projected climate change.
Integrated assessment models, pioneered by William Nordhaus, are now widely used to estimate regional and global climate damages under different policies.
Such models treat land, water and energy as production inputs; Herman Daly's early work replaced the circular flow diagram with one driven by solar energy.
Methods for counting environmental goods and services in national accounts are still debated.

related: Source and sink functions of the environment
distinct_from: Source and sink functions of the environment

title: Source and sink functions of the environment

definition.text: The environment's two economic roles: as a source that supplies materials and services, and as a sink that absorbs and neutralizes waste and pollution.

facts.text: Natural inputs pass out of the economy as pollution and waste once they are consumed.
The source function is depleted as resources are used up or polluted.
When waste exceeds the sink's capacity to absorb it, long-term damage follows.

definition.text: Short-run government and central-bank policy aimed at softening the harm done by business cycles, using fiscal and monetary tools.

facts.text: Policy is expansive in a recession and contractive when the economy overheats.
Longer-run structural policies instead target things like the structural unemployment rate or how much people save, invest and study.
Economists usually prefer monetary policy for moderate swings, since independent central banks face less political pressure and shorter lags.
Fiscal policy matters more after a major shock, in a liquidity trap, or under a fixed exchange rate.

definition.text: The reduction of private activity when government spending uses resources or raises interest rates, limiting fiscal policy's effect.

facts.text: Full crowding out happens when government spending simply replaces private output instead of adding to it.
Government spending that raises interest rates can also cut private investment.

definition.text: Parts of the tax and benefit system that cushion a downturn automatically, without new decisions by politicians.

facts.text: When unemployment rises, unemployment benefit spending rises and tax revenue falls, protecting part of private income and consumption.
They avoid the policy lags of discretionary fiscal policy.

definition.text: A common textbook model that finds the price level and real output where aggregate demand meets aggregate supply.

facts.text: The demand curve slopes down, so more output is demanded at lower price levels.
Near potential output, the full-employment level, extra demand only raises prices, not output.
Modern versions put inflation on the vertical axis, with an upward-sloping supply curve based on the Phillips curve.

definition.text: A model invented by John Hicks in 1936 showing the interest rates and output levels at which both the goods market and the money market are in balance.

facts.text: The goods market balances investment against saving (IS) and the money market balances money supply against money demand (LM).
It underpins the idea of aggregate demand by asking how much is demanded at a given price level.

definition.text: Branches of macroeconomics that reject mainstream theory, including ecological economics, modern monetary theory and Marxian economics.

facts.text: Heterodox economists see price flexibility, not price stickiness, as the source of instability, so they build models with different assumptions.

definition.text: The policy a nation's monetary authority uses to influence money and financial conditions in pursuit of goals such as high employment and low, stable inflation.

facts.text: Setting interest rates, directly or through open market operations, is generally its main tool.
Interest rate changes affect investment, consumption, asset prices and exchange rates, and so demand, employment and inflation; this is the monetary transmission mechanism.
Expansionary policy lowers rates to stimulate activity; contractionary policy dampens activity and inflation.
Most developed-country central banks target inflation, while most developing-country central banks target a fixed exchange rate.
Unlike fiscal policy, which uses taxes and government spending, it works through financial channels, and is usually run by central banks independent of government.
When interest rates are near zero, conventional policy cannot loosen further, so central banks may turn to quantitative easing.

title: Central bank
article: Monetary policy#Central banks and the gold standard

definition.text: A national bank that issues currency and sets interest rates, acting as lender of last resort to other banks.

facts.text: The Bank of England, created in 1694 with power to print gold-backed notes, began the idea of monetary policy independent of the executive.
Industrialized nations set up central banks between 1870 and 1920, the Federal Reserve among the last in 1913.
There is strong consensus that an independent central bank runs more credible monetary policy.

definition.text: A monetary policy strategy in which the central bank adjusts interest rates to keep inflation within an announced target range.

facts.text: New Zealand became the first country to adopt an official inflation target, in 1990.
Most developed-country central banks follow it, aiming for a target such as 2%, often flexibly so they can also steady output and jobs.
Clear communication is essential, because it shapes the inflation expectations that drive actual inflation.
After the 2008 crisis many economists argued the targets had been set too low.

definition.text: A central bank's buying and selling of securities to influence interest rates, the exchange rate or the money supply.

facts.text: Buying a security such as a government bond in effect creates money, expanding the monetary base; selling securities shrinks it.
The monetary base is currency in circulation plus banks' reserves held at the central bank.

title: Quantitative easing
article: Monetary policy#Unconventional monetary policy at the zero bound

definition.text: Unconventional monetary policy used when interest rates are near zero, in which the central bank buys bonds and other assets to lower a wider range of interest rates.

facts.text: Unconventional tools include credit easing, quantitative easing, forward guidance and signalling.
Purchases can include government bonds, corporate bonds, stocks and other securities.
It is used because conventional policy can fail in a liquidity trap.

definition.text: Central banks' adjustment of monetary and supervisory policy to account for the effects of climate change.

facts.text: Central banks began considering climate effects on their frameworks around 2017–2018.
They argue climate change will add market volatility, inflation pressure from extreme weather or a disorderly transition, and financial risks.
The Network for Greening the Financial System, founded in 2017, has more than a hundred central banks and supervisors.
Proposals include green macro-prudential rules, green quantitative easing, green collateral rules and green refinancing operations.
In 2021 the European Central Bank said it would tilt its corporate bond purchases, a form of green QE, but it has not adopted a green interest rate.
